query: How does Tantivy handle compression for string fast fields, and what's the relationship between the dictionary encoding and the u64 column representation?
chunk_content:
tantivy implements a few different compression codecs for the fast field columns, so it does a reasonable job there.

the place where things get a little strange is for string fast fields: tantivy uses a global dictionary per-segment, which means that the actual column is a u64 column, and is highly compressed using one of those codecs. the strings themselves in that dictionary are generically compressed, which isn't ideal... but because of the layout, they are (more) rarely needed.
validation_reason: The message directly addresses how Tantivy handles string fast fields, explaining that it uses a global dictionary per-segment that maps to u64 columns which are then compressed using codecs. It also explains the relationship between the dictionary encoding and u64 representation, noting that the strings in the dictionary are generically compressed while the u64 columns use specialized compression codecs.

query: hey does paradedb have like slow join performance or are they working on making joins faster?
chunk_content:
Hi <@U08FP3ZLBFC>. We've done a round of JOIN improvements in the past few months, but much of the work is left ahead. Today, JOINs in ParadeDB are fully executed by Postgres, meaning they process tuples "one at a time" (unlike other parts of our product which benefit from our columnar storage, processing tuples in batches).

We have plans for significant JOIN performance improvements, but it'll take us a few more months to execute on all of them. Thank you for your patience here :slightly_smiling_face:
validation_reason: The message directly addresses the query about ParadeDB's join performance, explaining that while they've made some improvements, joins are currently executed one tuple at a time by Postgres and they have plans for significant performance improvements in the coming months.

Any ongoing experiments on Vortex? Just curious

[Reply by unknown]
We did experiment with it. We know the Vortex team well and are excited for their project.

We ended up comparing the performance of vortex with our current columnar format. We found that there was not much difference and that much lower hanging fruits exist for improving aggregate performance in ParadeDB at the query execution level, so we haven’t adopted it yet

[Reply by unknown]
Thanks! Maybe no difference at the compression ratio as well?

[Reply by unknown]
tantivy implements a few different compression codecs for the fast field columns, so it does a reasonable job there.

the place where things get a little strange is for string fast fields: tantivy uses a global dictionary per-segment, which means that the actual column is a u64 column, and is highly compressed using one of those codecs. the strings themselves in that dictionary are generically compressed, which isn't ideal... but because of the layout, they are (more) rarely needed.

[Reply by unknown]
the performance is very good for the cases we're interested in, but as Phil said, there are a few changes we'd like to make in the medium term which might mean we explore it again.

Hi <@U08FP3ZLBFC>. We've done a round of JOIN improvements in the past few months, but much of the work is left ahead. Today, JOINs in ParadeDB are fully executed by Postgres, meaning they process tuples "one at a time" (unlike other parts of our product which benefit from our columnar storage, processing tuples in batches).

We have plans for significant JOIN performance improvements, but it'll take us a few more months to execute on all of them. Thank you for your patience here :slightly_smiling_face:

Hi <@U08FP3ZLBFC>. We've done a round of JOIN improvements in the past few months, but much of the work is left ahead. Today, JOINs in ParadeDB are fully executed by Postgres, meaning they process tuples "one at a time" (unlike other parts of our product which benefit from our columnar storage, processing tuples in batches).

We have plans for significant JOIN performance improvements, but it'll take us a few more months to execute on all of them. Thank you for your patience here :slightly_smiling_face:

chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
Hi, I’m trying to use BM25 in a TypeScript project, but it seems that the main ORMs don’t support the indexes. Is anyone using TypeScript who can provide guidance on how to work with it?

[Reply by unknown]
Hi <@U099AUM2V2S>! Yes, we'll be working on ORM support in the next few months, but for now it's not officially supported.

Some people have had success using libraries and writing full SQL commands, but it's not integrated with the ORM officially

[Reply by unknown]
I've done most of my integration using SQL commands inside helper functions.. happy to provide suggestions on how to implement without an ORM if you have questions!

[Reply by unknown]
What ORM are y'all using?

[Reply by unknown]
I'm using Sequelize, and been doing it like this without hacks
```{where: `"SeriesView"."id" @@@ '${JSON.stringify(q)}'::jsonb`}```
and just building the JSON query in JS and serialize to string

[Reply by unknown]
`Sequelize.literal()` can also do most of the logic needed, or `Sequelize.fn()` when calling functions with arguments

[Reply by unknown]
I use ActiveRecord on rails

[Reply by unknown]
Here is an example (in my model):

```def self.advanced_parade_search(query, category, page_token, where_clause = "1=1", params = [], limit = 10)
    # Prepare base SQL query components
    select_clause = <<~SQL.squish
      SELECT barcode, title, description, alt_title, category, brand, product_type,
              img_1_url, img_2_url, img_3_url, img_4_url, img_5_url, source,
              paradedb.score(barcode) as score
      FROM #{self.table_name}
    SQL

    if category.include?("&")
      where_clause_base = <<~SQL.squish
        WHERE (category = ?)
        AND (title @@@ ? OR alt_title @@@ ? OR description @@@ ?)
        AND (#{Arel.sql(where_clause)})
      SQL
    else
      where_clause_base = <<~SQL.squish
        WHERE (category @@@ ?)
        AND (title @@@ ? OR alt_title @@@ ? OR description @@@ ?)
        AND (#{Arel.sql(where_clause)})
      SQL
    end

    order_clause = "ORDER BY paradedb.score(barcode) DESC, barcode DESC"
    limit_clause = "LIMIT ?"

    if page_token.blank?
      # Default query (no page_token)
      sql = <<~SQL.squish
        #{select_clause}
        #{where_clause_base}
        #{order_clause}
        #{limit_clause}
      SQL

      query_params = [category, query, query, query, *params, limit]
    else
      # Decode page_token
      begin
        last_score, last_barcode = Base64.decode64(page_token).split('_')
        last_score = last_score.to_f
        raise 'Invalid page token format' unless last_score && last_barcode
        Rails.logger.debug("Paging cursor: score=#{last_score}, barcode=#{last_barcode}")
      rescue ArgumentError, TypeError
        raise 'Invalid page token: unable to decode or parse'
      end

      # Query with cursor-based pagination
      sql = <<~SQL.squish
        #{select_clause}
        #{where_clause_base}
        AND (paradedb.score(barcode) <= ? OR (paradedb.score(barcode) <= ? AND barcode <= ?))
        #{order_clause}
        #{limit_clause}
      SQL
      query_params = [category, query, query, query, *params, last_score, last_score, last_barcode, limit]
    end

    # Log the generated SQL and parameters
    Rails.logger.debug("Executing SQL: #{sql}")
    Rails.logger.debug("Parameters: #{query_params.inspect}")

    # Execute query
    async_find_by_sql([sql, *query_params])
  end```

query: Hey folks, might be a dumb question but how do I check if my columns are set up as fast fields in ParadeDB? I'm trying to understand why some of our aggregations after search are slower than expected and want to make sure we configured things right. Also wondering what the process is if we need to change that setting - do we have to rebuild the whole index?
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
*Question 2 – Verifying fast fields for post‑search aggregates*

I included a numeric rating column in the BM25 index so I can quickly facet after search:

`SELECT review_rating, COUNT(*)`
`FROM hepsi_reviews`
`WHERE review_body @@@ 'kargo'`
`GROUP BY 1;`

Questions:

• How do I confirm that column is actually stored as a fast field? (Is there a flag in _*paradedb.schema('<index_name>')*_ I should look at?)
• If a column is not fast, what performance difference should I expect on large result sets?
• What’s the recommended way to “promote” an existing column to fast field—drop & re‑create the index, or is there an ALTER / rebuild path?


[Reply by unknown]
> • How do I confirm that column is actually stored as a fast field? (Is there a flag in _*paradedb.schema('<index_name>')*_ I should look at?)
yes: `fast`, iirc?

[Reply by unknown]
> • If a column is not fast, what performance difference should I expect on large result sets?
in EXPLAIN, you will see a `Normal` scan rather than a `FastField*` scan

the performance difference between the two depends on the width of the row:

if you have a very narrow row, then getting the row from Postgres' heap isn't so bad, because most of each fetch actually pulls in data that you need (not much of the read is wasted on columns you're not using.)

if you have a very wide row, then (modulo TOAST), getting the row from columnar storage can be much more dense, because you're fetching _exactly_ that column contiguously.

[Reply by unknown]
it also depends how much your WHERE clause eliminates: if the result is a small fraction of the total, then the per-row density doesn't matter as much, because you'll rarely get the advantage of read-ahead (where fetching one row conveniently also buffers the next one for you)

[Reply by unknown]
> • What’s the recommended way to “promote” an existing column to fast field—drop & re‑create the index, or is there an ALTER / rebuild path?
there is only re-creating... but i think that the recommended approach is with `REINDEX`...?

[Reply by unknown]
oh, actually: possible create a new `*_v2` index concurrently, and then drop the old one.

[Reply by unknown]

I’ll check the fast flag in paradedb.schema(...), watch for FastField vs Normal in EXPLAIN, keep row width + selectivity in mind for perf, and rebuild via REINDEX (or create *_v2 concurrently then drop) if I need to promote fields.
I’ll run a few tests on my dataset and report back numbers if that’s useful. Appreciate the detailed guidance!

> • If a column is not fast, what performance difference should I expect on large result sets?
in EXPLAIN, you will see a `Normal` scan rather than a `FastField*` scan

the performance difference between the two depends on the width of the row:

if you have a very narrow row, then getting the row from Postgres' heap isn't so bad, because most of each fetch actually pulls in data that you need (not much of the read is wasted on columns you're not using.)

if you have a very wide row, then (modulo TOAST), getting the row from columnar storage can be much more dense, because you're fetching _exactly_ that column contiguously.

query: Given the technical context around pgvector's HNSW index limitations—specifically the pre-filtering issue where HNSW performs index search first, returns a maximum of ~1,000 results, and only then applies filters (which creates problems in multi-tenant scenarios where team-specific vectors might not appear in the initial result set due to the result limit)—and considering that we're evaluating vector search solutions for our compliance documentation system that requires strict tenant isolation per SOC 2 requirements: Does ParadeDB implement any architectural modifications or alternative indexing strategies to pgvector's standard HNSW implementation that would address the pre-filtering limitation, or does it rely on pgvector's native HNSW behavior? I need to understand this for our security architecture review, as we cannot risk cross-tenant data exposure in search results due to the filtering order-of-operations issue described in the TigerData blog post (https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/how-we-built-a-content-recommendation-system-with-pgai-and-pgvectorscale).
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
I was just reading about `pgvector` & how it uses `HSNW` index & its limitations. I assume ParadeDB already handles this? How do we really get around this limitation?

<https://www.tigerdata.com/blog/how-we-built-a-content-recommendation-system-with-pgai-and-pgvectorscale>
> 1. HNSW index-based searches can't take advantage of pre-filtering in a meaningful way. Searching for vectors with HNSW always first runs the index search, fetches the results, and only then applies the filter. To add insult to injury, HNSW can only return a maximum amount of results from the search (less than 1,000 in most cases, otherwise it gets quite slow). query: Given the documented behavior of ParadeDB's ngram tokenizer with min_gram=3 and max_gram=3, what explains the divergent matching semantics between the `@@@` operator with bare string literals versus `paradedb.match()` function calls, and what are the specific tokenization rules regarding whitespace handling that cause unexpected matches against terms like "MORGAN STANLEY & CO INTERNATIONAL PLC" when querying for "Coca Cola"?
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
Hi, we've been running into a result we weren't quite expecting when doing name matching. See the query:
```SELECT issuer_name, paradedb.score(isin) from bonds_reference
WHERE isin @@@ paradedb.match('issuer_name', 'Coca Cola')
ORDER BY score DESC```
And here's the `condition` for the index:
```(key_field=isin, text_fields='{
        "issuer_name": {
          "tokenizer": {"type": "ngram", "min_gram": 3, "max_gram": 3, "prefix_only": false}
        }
    }')```
The query returns results like:
```INDUSTRIAL AND COMMERCIAL BANK OF CHINA MACAU LIMITED
MORGAN STANLEY & CO INTERNATIONAL PLC```
However, since min and max gram are both 3, I would expect these to not match, as neither contain: coc, oca, col, ola. What's the reason for matches on these occurring?

[Reply by unknown]
The ParadeDB team will be able to help more but if nGrams here work anything like nGrams in other systems grams they add space before and after the first and last letter.

coca would give you the following grams
"c","co","coc""oca","ca" "a"

That could be the cause?

[Reply by unknown]
<@U05MP5P030R> any idea here?

[Reply by unknown]
One more note about this. The reason I assumed the only ngrams matched would be "coc", "oca", "col", "ola" is because when using:
```issuer_name @@@ 'Coca Cola'```
We got the result as expected; in other words, names with only those ngrams were the ones that got matched. So these two syntaxes have different behaviour. I'm not completely clear on why this is the case.

[Reply by unknown]
Yea `issuer_name @@@ 'Coca Cola'` is most definitely not the same query as `isin @@@ paradedb.match('issuer_name', 'Coca Cola')`

[Reply by unknown]
You can see what the tokens are like so:

```SELECT token AS tokens 
FROM paradedb.tokenize(
  paradedb.tokenizer('ngram', min_gram=>3, max_gram=>3, prefix_only=>false),
  'Coca Cola'
);
 tokens 
--------
 coc
 oca
 ca 
 a c
  co
 col
 ola
(7 rows)```


[Reply by unknown]
And you can see the intersection like this:

```SELECT token AS tokens 
FROM paradedb.tokenize(
  paradedb.tokenizer('ngram', min_gram=>3, max_gram=>3, prefix_only=>false),
  'Coca Cola'
) 
INTERSECT

SELECT token AS tokens 
FROM paradedb.tokenize(
  paradedb.tokenizer('ngram', min_gram=>3, max_gram=>3, prefix_only=>false),
  'MORGAN STANLEY & CO INTERNATIONAL PLC'
) ;

 tokens 
--------
  co
(1 row)```

[Reply by unknown]
Yes, we figured, but this is a highly unusual default setting for an ngram tokenizer isn't it?

[Reply by unknown]
Including spaces as part of the raw string to be tokenized leads to very unintended results

[Reply by unknown]
I tried to wrangle the regex tokenizer to achieve a custom 3-gram implementation that ignores non-alphanumeric characters but it seems that the paradedb regex does not support lookahead operators (which are needed to implement overlapping 3-grams)

[Reply by unknown]
Additionally, can you provide some clarity on the difference between  `issuer_name @@@ 'Coca Cola'` and `isin @@@ paradedb.match('issuer_name', 'Coca Cola')` ? Per the documentation they seem to be equivalent but the results are actually not equivalent

[Reply by unknown]
Hi Miguel! I’m at a conference this week, so a bit slower to respond. Two things:

1- You are right that some of our defaults are not ideal right now. In fact we’re revamping how our tokenizers are defined as we speak. I expect this will ship in a few weeks at most and should fix this problem once and for all. Apologies for the inconvenience here.

2- I’ll chat with the team about the specific match query and get back to you 

[Reply by unknown]
Thank you for your patience and valuable feedback!

[Reply by unknown]
Padding rules vary amongst n-gram tokenizers, but padding is customary. Some tools let you configure the padding rules, most don’t. Padding improves candidate selection in many cases.

Doesn’t mean it’s the right default for your case, obviously.

[Reply by unknown]
We've got new defaults coming soon :slightly_smiling_face: Stay tuned!

It demonstrates through examples that whitespace is included in ngram tokenization, showing how 'co' becomes a token that causes matches with 'MORGAN STANLEY & CO'. The thread also confirms these are different queries: 'issuer_name @@@ 'Coca Cola'' vs 'isin @@@ paradedb.match('issuer_name', 'Coca Cola')' though the full explanation of why they differ is pending from the ParadeDB team.

query: how do u version paradedb indexs without teh long matview rebuild times? current setup taking forever w 70gb data
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
how should we go about _versioning_ different tables / indexes for paradedb?

ATM I have my raw data in individual tables, and create a materialized view with a version number (paradedb indexes are created on top of these materialized views). this was working OK but now we're getting painfully long materialized view build times (as it's about 70 gb of data and the operation is a UNION ALL of >12 different tables).

is there something better i could do? using neon's built-in branching is an option, but significantly more expensive than standard RDS offerings so (we'd about 6x our costs).

[Reply by unknown]
if ya'll don't need versioning, `pg_ivm` could be of use? Though your write throughput could take a hit

[Reply by unknown]
We tried pg_ivm, and it's a disaster for our app which is 50% read / 50% write.
Why not having index on each table ? I think I have read that paradedb is working on joins search. But it already works ok.

[Reply by unknown]
Most of our customers version indexes via the name they give to it and use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to build a new index version without interrupting usage of the existing one.

As Quentin mentioned, you should be able to do that directly on the regular tables, without needing materialized views.

[Reply by unknown]
Hmm but I assume one index being created immediately deletes the prior index in that case <@U05MP5P030R>? at least i recall "only one bm25 index is allowed" errors in the past.

My current workflow is :
1. run my data ingestion pipeline (typically augments data to the tables, sometimes overwrites them completely, is declarative so could overwrite everything if needed) 
2. create the new materialized view (+ indexes) 
3. run a set of checks to ensure all the data that i expect is present 
4. switch production to `paradedb_query_table_1_35` over from `paradedb_query_table_1_34`
 likely a strange case of a paradedb user as i'm not actually searching data that's already in postgres anyways and it is the result of an ingestion pipeline.

i'm primarily using paradedb so:
• i can use mostly-postgres to do the job instead of having to learn something different. 
• i could give an LLM access to higher level querying tools (i.e. "count the number of documents that have the word $TEXT or company $COMPANY" or "find all recalls from company $COMPANY across these 5 different countries/datasets" 
albeit maybe the limitations are showing here, from my chatgpt conversations neon+paradedb should enable cost-less-ish versioning and this is cloning is also a much faster operation with elastic.

definitely open to a brief call with someone if you all have time to discuss i may also be describing this stuff poorly. side project that's gathering traction so now i have to fix this...

[Reply by unknown]
For this kind of versioning, likely what you'd want is the branching model that Neon offers. Doing this at the level of the ParadeDB extension is out of scope

query:
I'm investigating a discrepancy in search result counts between ParadeDB's `paradedb.parse()` function and the `match` JSON format when processing user-supplied boolean search queries containing AND/OR/NOT operators. Specifically, I'm working with ParadeDB version [assuming latest stable] on PostgreSQL [version], querying a `profiles` table with full-text search capabilities.

**Environment Details:**
- Database: PostgreSQL with ParadeDB extension
- Table: `public.profiles` with fields including `group_id`, `search_string`, `headline`, and `deleted_at`
- Search operators in user query: AND, OR, NOT with quoted phrases
- Index type: [assuming BM25 or similar full-text index]

**Observed Behavior:**
When executing what should be equivalent queries, I'm seeing dramatically different result counts:
- `paradedb.parse()`: 4 rows returned in 48ms
- JSON `match` format: 11,486 rows returned in 245ms

**What I've Already Investigated:**
1. Verified both queries filter on the same `group_id` value
2. Confirmed both exclude soft-deleted records (`deleted_at IS NULL`)
3. Attempted to replicate the boolean logic structure in JSON format
4. Reviewed ParadeDB documentation on query syntax differences

**My Question:**
What is the correct approach for handling user-provided boolean search strings (containing AND/OR/NOT operators) in ParadeDB when using the JSON match format, and what are the architectural or security reasons that the JSON match format does not natively parse boolean operators the way `paradedb.parse()` does?
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
Tantivy parse seems to handle a user boolean search query (AND / OR / NOT ) and I cannot have match handle it. Am I missing something ?

*Tantivy : 4 rows, 48ms*
```    SELECT count(*)
    FROM public.profiles p
    WHERE p @@@ paradedb.parse(
        'group_id:"952582b4-bb51-461e-b566-0e5f980f4660" AND (' ||
            'search_string:(recruteur AND "talent acquisition" AND recruit)^3 OR ' ||
            'headline:(recruteur AND "talent acquisition" AND recruit)' ||
        ')'
    )
    AND p.deleted_at IS NULL```
*match JSON format : 11486 rows, 245ms*
```    SELECT count(*)
    FROM public.profiles p, parameters params
    WHERE p @@@ jsonb_build_object(
        'boolean', jsonb_build_object(
            'must', jsonb_build_array(
                jsonb_build_object('term', jsonb_build_object('field', 'group_id', 'value', '952582b4-bb51-461e-b566-0e5f980f4660')),
                jsonb_build_object('boolean', jsonb_build_object('should', jsonb_build_array(
                    jsonb_build_object('match', jsonb_build_object('field', 'search_string', 'value', 'recruteur AND "talent acquisition" AND recruit', 'boost', 3)),
                    jsonb_build_object('match', jsonb_build_object('field', 'headline', 'value', 'recruteur AND "talent acquisition" AND recruit'))
                )))
            )
        )
    )
    AND p.deleted_at IS NULL```
How would you handle complex search strings provided by users ?
And why do you recommand not using the Tantivy query string directly ?

[Reply by unknown]
If the user is typing in AND/OR/NOT themselves, using `paradedb.parse` is fine

[Reply by unknown]
`paradedb.parse` uses Tantivy's query parser, `match` does not

```The error paradedb ERROR: could not find function text_support_wrapper indicates that the PostgreSQL server cannot find a required function within the pg_search.so library. This is typically caused by a version mismatch or a corrupted installation of the ParadeDB extension. 
Common causes and solutions
Installation or upgrade issues
If you have recently installed or upgraded ParadeDB, the pg_search extension might not have been created or updated correctly. The error is common after an upgrade because the old extension binary may still be active. 
Solution: Follow the official ParadeDB documentation for upgrading. If the issue persists, you may need to drop and re-create the extension.
Caution: Dropping the extension will remove any indexes that depend on it.
DROP EXTENSION pg_search CASCADE;
CREATE EXTENSION pg_search; 
Version conflicts
Different versions of ParadeDB might have slight differences in their function signatures or the way they are compiled, especially when running a self-hosted installation. 
Solution: Ensure that your pg_search.so file and the ParadeDB extension versions are compatible with your PostgreSQL version (in this case, PostgreSQL 17). Verify the extension version by running SELECT * FROM paradedb.version_info();. 
Incorrect shared library preload settings
For PostgreSQL versions older than 17, pg_search must be explicitly added to shared_preload_libraries in the postgresql.conf file. While unnecessary for PostgreSQL 17, an incorrect or mismatched entry could still cause problems. 
Solution: If using an older version of Postgres, confirm that the postgresql.conf file includes shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_search'. For Postgres 17, check that there are no conflicting or incorrectly configured entries. 
Corrupted or missing binary file
The pg_search.so file itself may be corrupted, or the PostgreSQL server may be looking for the library in the wrong location. 
Solution: Reinstall ParadeDB to ensure the binary files are installed correctly. For containerized or self-hosted installations, you may need to enter the container or use apt-get install to install or repair the prebuilt binaries. ```
